newsitem.title: CANADA: High-speed clouds said raw material for Milky Way.
newsitem.headline: High-speed clouds said raw material for Milky Way.

text.p: Mysterious clouds speeding around the Milky Way galaxy could be remnants of the galactic birth process but could also provide the raw material for future stars, astronomers said on Tuesday.

Hydrogen clouds, discovered decades ago but never explained, move about twice as fast as the Sun orbits the centre of the Milky Way and are "placental remains" of the galaxy's birth, according to Leo Blitz of the University of California-Berkeley.

While these high-velocity clouds (HVCs) moved in the area of the Milky Way and the larger neighbouring Andromeda galaxy, they were not part of either galaxy, he told a news conference at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society in Toronto.
"They were moving so fast they couldn't be part of the galactic plain," Blitz said.

Discovered in the 1960s, the clouds have puzzled scientists, especially when they were found to be moving toward the centre of both the Milky Way and Andromeda at a ferocious rate -- about 310 miles (500 km) per second.

Using telescopes in Argentina, the Netherlands and the United States, as well as computer simulations, Blitz and his fellow researchers found that HVCs were the "mine" from which the stars and planets of our galaxy were built.

"What we're seeing here is the material that's ... going to continue to be the future fuel for star-formation in the Milky Way. If this picture is right this is going to be the gas that'll turn into stars a billion years into the future," David Spergel of Princeton University, who was part of the research team, said.

HVCs may also be some of the first structures to form in the universe, the astronomers said, theorising that small objects formed soon after the universe was born merged with other objects to form larger systems, including galaxies.
HVCs could be the "basic building block" of galaxies, the astronomers said.

Another possibility is that the clouds may contain "dark matter," a non-luminous material thought to be the repository for most of the mass of the universe. If they do contain "dark matter" they could help scientists determine just what it is.

Even though the high-speed clouds are not very dense, they contain vast amounts of mass: about 10 billion times the mass of the Sun. These fast-moving clouds have nothing to do with the Great Magellanic Cloud, which may be the leftovers from a defunct galaxy near the Milky Way, the scientists said.
